summary: Describes a simple extension to TFTP, the Trivial File Transfer Protocol, that lets a client and server negotiate options before a transfer begins. It is a draft standard.

plainLanguage.summary: TFTP moves a file one small block at a time, and it has no way to negotiate anything on the way. This document adds a short handshake at the start: the client lists the options it would like, such as a block size of 1432 bytes, the server answers with the options it agrees to and the values it will use, and the transfer then runs with those settings. An option the server does not mention is simply not used.

subtitle: A small extension to TFTP that lets a client and a server agree on options, such as block size, before a transfer starts.

tldr.problem: TFTP is a lock-step file transfer protocol with no way for the two ends to agree on anything before the transfer starts, so a client cannot ask for a larger block size or a different timeout.
tldr.mechanism: The client appends options to the Read or Write Request, and a server that supports negotiation answers with a new packet type, the Option Acknowledgment, listing the options it accepts and the values it will use. An option the server does not acknowledge is ignored by both ends.
tldr.outcome: The document defines the request and OACK formats, the negotiation rules and a new TFTP error code, 8, for a transfer that has to be stopped. It was created to carry the blocksize option and is the base for the timeout option as well.

facts.label: Options in one request
facts.value: Any number, but each option only once

today: RFC 2347 is a Draft Standard from May 1998 and has not been obsoleted. It updated RFC 1350 and obsoleted RFC 1782. The negotiation mechanism it defines is the base that the blocksize and timeout options in RFC 2348 and RFC 2349 are built on.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Trivial File Transfer Protocol is a simple, lock-step file transfer protocol that lets a client get a file onto or off a remote host. This document describes a simple extension to TFTP that allows option negotiation before the file transfer.

The mechanism is a backward-compatible extension to TFTP. It lets transfer options be negotiated before the transfer, using a mechanism consistent with TFTP's request packet format. It is kept simple by enforcing a request, respond, acknowledge sequence, similar to the lock-step approach TFTP itself takes.

The mechanism is general purpose, in that many kinds of option may be negotiated, but it was created to support the blocksize option defined in RFC 2348. Additional options are defined in RFC 2349.
sections.plainLanguage: TFTP is a simple protocol that copies a file a block at a time. This document lets the two ends agree on a few settings before the copying starts, without changing the protocol itself, so a server that does not know about options still works exactly as before.

sections.title: Packet Formats
sections.content:
TFTP options are appended to the Read Request and Write Request packets, after the file name and the transfer mode. A new type of TFTP packet, the Option Acknowledgment (OACK), is used to acknowledge a client's option negotiation request. A new error code, 8, is defined to indicate that a transfer should be terminated because of option negotiation.

In the request, the opcode field contains either a 1, for a Read Request, or 2, for a Write Request. The file name is the name of the file to be read or written, and the mode is the mode of the transfer, netascii, octet or mail. Both are NULL-terminated fields. The options follow: the first option, such as blksize, is a NULL-terminated field in case-insensitive ASCII, followed by its value, also NULL-terminated and in case-insensitive ASCII, and then any further option and value pairs. All the options and values are NULL-terminated, in keeping with the original request format. If multiple options are to be negotiated they are appended to each other, and the order in which they are given is not significant. The maximum size of a request packet is 512 octets.

The OACK packet holds the opcode 6, for Option Acknowledgment, followed by the acknowledged options. The first option acknowledgment is copied from the original request, and its value is the acknowledged value for that option; how and whether that value may differ from the requested one is a matter for the specification of the individual option. Further option and value acknowledgment pairs follow, each one NULL-terminated.
sections.plainLanguage: The request keeps its old shape and grows a list of options at the end, each one a name and a value separated by a zero byte. The server answers with a packet whose opcode is 6, listing the options it accepts. A request may not be larger than 512 bytes, which is the same limit the original protocol had.

sections.title: Negotiation Protocol
sections.content:
The client appends the options to the end of the Read Request or Write Request. Any number of options may be specified, but an option may only be specified once, and the order of the options is not significant.

If the server supports option negotiation and recognises one or more of the options in the request, the server may respond with an Option Acknowledgment. Each option that the server recognises, and accepts the value for, is included in the OACK. Some options allow an alternate value to be proposed, but that is a feature of the individual option. The server must not include in the OACK any option that the client did not specifically request: only the client may initiate option negotiation. Options that the server does not support are omitted from the OACK and do not cause an ERROR packet. If the value of a supported option is invalid, the specification for that option says whether the server should simply omit the option, respond with an alternate value, or send an ERROR packet with error code 8 to terminate the transfer.

An option that the server does not acknowledge must be ignored by the client and the server as if it had never been requested. If several options were requested, the client must use the ones that were acknowledged and must not use the ones that were not.

When the client appends options to a Read Request, the server may answer with an OACK, acknowledging the request and the options, with a DATA packet, acknowledging the request but not the options, or with an ERROR packet, meaning the request has been denied. When the client appends options to a Write Request, the server may answer with an OACK, with an ACK acknowledging the request but not the options, or with an ERROR packet.

A server that does not support option negotiation will likely ignore any options appended to the request, and will return a DATA packet for a Read Request and an ACK packet for a Write Request, establishing a normal TFTP data transfer. If such a server returns an error for a request that carries an option, the client may repeat the request without appending any options, which handles servers that treat the extra data as an error.

There are two ways for the client to confirm that it accepts the server's OACK. If the transfer was started with a Read Request, the client sends an ACK with the data block number set to 0 to confirm the values in the OACK. If the transfer was started with a Write Request, the client begins the transfer with the first DATA packet, using the negotiated values. If the client rejects the OACK, it sends an ERROR packet with error code 8 and the transfer is terminated. Once the client has acknowledged an OACK with an appropriate non-error response, it has agreed to use only the options and values the server returned. The server cannot request an option, it can only respond to them. If the client receives an OACK containing an option it did not ask for, it should respond with an ERROR packet with error code 8 and terminate the transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the client starts the negotiation, and the server may only answer with options that were asked for. An option the server leaves out is treated as if it had never been proposed, and it must not cause an error. The client then either confirms with a zero-numbered acknowledgement or starts sending data, and from that point both ends use the server's answers.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The document gives two worked exchanges, both negotiating the blksize option.

In the read example the client sends a Read Request for the file foofile in octet mode with the option blksize and the value 1432. The server replies with an OACK carrying blksize 1432. The client sends an ACK with block number 0, and the server then sends the data blocks, each of 1432 octets, each acknowledged in turn by the client.

In the write example the client sends a Write Request for the file barfile in octet mode with the option blksize and the value 2048. The server replies with an OACK carrying blksize 2048. The client then sends the data blocks, each of 2048 octets, and the server acknowledges each one.
sections.plainLanguage: In the read example the client asks for 1432-byte blocks, the server agrees, and the file arrives in blocks of that size with the usual acknowledgement after each one. In the write example the client asks for 2048-byte blocks and starts sending data straight away once the server has agreed, with no separate confirmation of the OACK.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The basic TFTP protocol has no security mechanism, which is why it has no rename, delete or file overwrite capabilities. This document does not add any security to TFTP, and the extensions it specifies do not add any additional security risks.
sections.plainLanguage: TFTP has no security of its own, which is why it cannot rename or delete files. This document adds no security and no new risk either.

items.title: Only the client asks
items.text: The server may not include an option the client did not request.

items.title: Unknown options are skipped
items.text: An option the server does not support is left out of the OACK, and does not cause an error.

items.title: Unacknowledged means unused
items.text: Both ends ignore an option the server did not acknowledge.

items.title: Alternate values are allowed
items.text: An individual option may let the server answer with a different value.

items.title: One round trip
items.text: The client confirms with an acknowledgement, or simply starts sending data.

items.title: Error code 8 stops it
items.text: A rejected OACK, or one naming an unrequested option, ends the transfer.
